newsitem.title: UK: Five year UK gilt auction result disappoints.
newsitem.headline: Five year UK gilt auction result disappoints.

text.p: UK gilts lost some ground on Wednesday after the Bank of England said its five year gilt auction was covered 1.70 times.
"The bid to cover was disappointing...and less than the previous two auctions," DKB economist Gerard Lyons told RFTV.
The Bank said its auction of 2.5 billion sterling of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002 had a yield tail of two basis points and a price tail of 3/32.
By 1100 GMT December gilts were down 19/32 on the day at 111-12 from 111-14 just prior to the auction results.
BZW gilts analyst Kevin Adams said the five year area of the curve was quite good value before the auction. "One might have expected a better turn out than the 1.70 cover we saw," he said.
Analysts said the cover was particularly disappointing when compared to that in the two previous five year gilt auctions where it was 3.57 and 2.64 times.
The gilt market has been riding high recently, making new contract highs on three consecutive trading days.
But worries about further interest rate rises and sterling's dramatic drop overnight encouraged some profit taking, dealers said.
Societe Generale analyst Tom Rayner said weak overseas demand for the stock may have contributed to the small cover.
"I don't suppose the collapse in sterling yesterday helped international sentiment much -- the biggest drop in the currency since we came out of the ERM," he said.
The pound tumbled eight pfennigs on Tuesday from its four year high of 2.6370 marks but had hauled itself back slightly by the European midsession.
"Gilts don't take that much notice of sterling...but to the extent our and the U.S. markets were helped by the currency, this turnaround won't be too helpful at this point," said Adams.
Lyons said the market should have no trouble absorbing the remaining 9.4 billion sterling worth of gilts to be issued between now and the end of March.
"It's not a heavy load of supply and in the international environment it should be lapped up even though this morning's auction was disappointing," he said.
"Basically, I think gilts look good but not just yet. There is going to be a lot of good news around partly because there is too much bad news being discounted in the market," he added.
Wednesday's 7.0 percent stock due 2002 will be the new five year benchmark.
Dealers said Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's monetary policy meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George on December 11 would provide the next major stumbling block for gilts.
Analysts are split over the likelihood of a pre-Christmas rate hike.

Andrew Davies from London Bond Broking expects Clarke to raise rates by 25 basis points from their present 6.0 percent at the meeting. "In the electoral timetable I think it's a good time to do it because by the time of the election people will have forgotten about it," he said.
But Adams said a new year rate rise was more likely.
"To raise rates quite so soon after the budget would suggest his budget judgement was wrong and I don't think he wants to put that across," Adams said.
The March short sterling contract was down one basis point at 93.29 by 1145 GMT, suggesting official interest rates of around 6.71 percent by the end of the first quarter next year.
